turns.content: It's 2am and I'm still at the office. Not working — just sitting. The bridge round officially died on Tuesday. Rohit and Sneha put in their papers this week, which honestly, smart. Four months of runway if I stop taking salary, which I already have. I built this thing for five years.

Oh man, I’m so sorry. That’s a *lot* to carry all at once—especially at 2 AM, when the office feels like a ghost town and the weight of it all just *sits* there with you. Five years is a huge chunk of your life to pour into something, and watching it unravel like this… that’s not just a professional gut-punch, it’s a personal one too.

I’m guessing part of you is relieved, in a weird way? Like, the uncertainty is finally over, even if the outcome sucks. But another part of you is probably replaying every decision, every “what if,” like a broken record. And losing Rohit and Sneha on top of it—people you built this *with*—that’s got to sting extra.

What’s going through your head right now? Are you mad? Numb? Already thinking about what’s next? (And more importantly—have you eaten anything today, or are you running on caffeine and existential dread?)

The worst part is the performance. Every standup I'm doing this voice — confident, "we have irons in the fire" — and everyone knows. My co-founder knows. The two juniors who stayed definitely know, they're staying out of loyalty and I'm burning their careers for it. At home I do a different voice. I'm so tired of my own voices, man.

Ugh, that performance piece is *exhausting*—like you’re the CEO of a company that’s already closed, just going through the motions for an audience that isn’t even buying it. That voice you’re putting on? It’s armor, but it’s also a prison. You’re carrying the weight of the illusion for everyone else, and it’s *draining* you.

And those two juniors? That guilt is real. They’re staying because they believe in *you*, not the company, and that’s a heavy thing to hold. But also—maybe they’re learning more about resilience and loyalty in these last few months than they would in a year at a stable job. Not that it makes it okay, but it’s not nothing.

What would happen if you let the voice crack just a little? Not a full meltdown, but like… “Hey, this is hard, and I’m figuring it out too”? Would that feel like failure, or relief? (And—side note—how’s your co-founder holding up? Are they in the same spiral, or are they checked out?)

Please don't give me ideas. I know all the ideas. I've read every pivot thread, I've drafted the down-round email six times, I know about bridge financing and acquihires and "focusing on revenue". I know. I just need to say this somewhere: I am scared, and I can't say it in any room I'm in.

I hear you. And I’m not here to fix it—you’ve already done the homework, the spreadsheets, the scenario planning. You’re not scared because you don’t know the options; you’re scared because *none of them feel like winning*. That’s a different kind of fear. It’s the kind that sits in your chest like a stone, the kind that doesn’t get smaller when you name it—it just gets heavier because now it’s real.

You don’t have to say it in any of those rooms. You don’t have to perform strength for the board, or optimism for the team, or detachment for your co-founder. You can just… be scared here. For as long as you need. No one’s grading you on how fast you bounce back. Five years is a long time to love something that’s slipping through your fingers. That grief doesn’t disappear just because the runway does.

I’m here. Say it again if you need to. Or don’t. We can just sit in the quiet too.

Is it over? Like actually — you can be honest. Five years. My dad still tells people I have a "computer business". Some nights I want it to just end so I can stop performing, and then I hate myself for wanting that. Then I open the metrics dashboard again like it's going to say something new at 2am.

Yeah. It’s over.
Not in the dramatic, fiery crash way—more like a slow deflation. The kind where you keep checking the gauge, hoping the needle will twitch, but it just… doesn’t. Five years is a long time to outlast your own hope, and the dashboard isn’t going to whisper some secret at 2 AM that it hasn’t already said a hundred times before.

Your dad’s “computer business” line is heartbreaking in the best way—it’s love without understanding, the kind that keeps you warm even when it’s outdated. You don’t have to rip that Band-Aid off for him yet. Let him keep saying it a little longer. You’ve earned that grace.

And that cycle—wanting it to end, hating yourself for wanting it, then opening the dashboard again—it’s not weakness. It’s just the last loops of a brain that’s still trying to solve a puzzle that’s already been boxed up. You’re allowed to want the performance to stop. You’re also allowed to mourn it. Both can be true at the same time.
